Élections fédérales 2025 : Paroles queer: 2025 Federal Election: Queer Voices as the Vote Approaches
Comment on se sent en temps que personne: How does it feel to be a queer person during this election period?
La Converse continue à documenter le res: La Converse continues to document how communities are feeling during this election period. Aude, a colleague at La Converse, and I went to Café Velours, an establishment well known to members of the LGBTQ+ community in the Villeray neighbourhood, to gather their impressions of how the campaign is going. The co-owner, Allison, welcomed us with open arms and explained, with great sincerity and transparency, how she feels about the current context. She put us in touch with staff members as well as customers who identify with this community and were willing to share their stories.
Nous nous sommes ensuite rendues rue Sai: We then headed to Sainte-Catherine Street, in the Village. I spoke with passersby on the street and customers in cafés. People were less comfortable sharing their comments or being filmed for the video segment. After a while, we realized that our collection of testimonies lacked diversity. So we focused on a wider range of profiles for this article.
Finalement, je suis satisfaite du portra: In the end, I am satisfied with the portrait of the situation that we can present to you today.
<strong>Villeray. Au Café Velours, plusi: Villeray. At Café Velours, several customers are having a coffee or tea and studying, reading a book or talking in low voices. The place is peaceful and fairly full. The setting is conducive to conversation. We approach them with one question: how does it feel to be a queer person during this election period?
Un désintérêt global est manifeste chez: A general disinterest is evident among everyone we interviewed. They all seem to have accepted that their voices are not, and probably will not be, heard in this campaign. They all describe a sense of detachment from the parties in the running. Unsurprisingly, they identify little or not at all with the politicians’ speeches. Despite it all, most will go vote on April 28.
<strong>ALLISON : « Les enjeux qui touch: ALLISON: “The issues affecting the queer community are the same as those affecting the middle class”
Allison est co-propriétaire du Café Velo: Allison is a co-owner of Café Velours. When we arrive, she is chatting with a regular on the outdoor terrace. Wearing a red hooded jacket and a cap, she answers our questions energetically.
C’est la première à dénoncer le manque d: She is the first to denounce the lack of representation in federal politics, a subject that will come up in every interview. “I feel there aren’t enough politicians, whether they’re queer or not, who deal with subjects like access to housing, access to health care or even access to general services for the LGBTQ+ community,” she says.
Dans son ton, on sent une implication ci: In her tone, you can feel a strong commitment to civic life. She names the Palestinian genocide as her main political concern. It is the first thing she looked at in the various party platforms. Next, everything related to daily life goes under her magnifying glass.
« Les enjeux qui touchent la communauté: “The issues affecting the queer community are the same as those affecting the middle class, the working class. We’re talking about housing, health, safety, employment,” she explains. “The restrictions on freedom that affect queer people are often the same as those that affect women, people with disabilities and many others.”
Quand on lui parle du sentiment de sécur: When we ask her about the overall sense of safety in Canada, she answers that she knows she is in a position of privilege. The political situation among our neighbours to the south worries her greatly. “I see how hard we fight, body and soul, for the rights of women, immigrants, queer people, and that we could lose everything overnight,” says Allison. “We see American fascism growing and gaining momentum. We don’t want that for ourselves.”
<strong>FRANKIEB : « J’ai l’impression q: FRANKIEB: “I feel like most of the actions being taken are performative”
FrankieB s’installe sur un divan au Café: FrankieB settles onto a couch at Café Velours, where we arranged to meet. FrankieB is dressed in black, wears glasses with bold frames, has painted nails and several piercings visible on their face. FrankieB assures us: on the street, people turn around when they walk by.
Se sentant privilégié de pouvoir exercer: Feeling privileged to be able to exercise their right to vote, but not feeling that their vote will change much, FrankieB is hesitant to vote. An activist involved in the queer community, they believe their volunteer work has more impact than going to the polls on April 28. “I find that, in general, politics is not accessible. This world lacks plain-language explanation. I find it complicated to follow the campaign and figure out how the parties’ decisions will affect my future.”
Encore une fois, FrankieB ne se sent pas: Once again, FrankieB does not feel concerned by this campaign: “I feel like our voices aren’t really listened to, and when they are, it’s in a tokenized* way. I feel like most of the actions being taken are performative.”
Iel évoque ensuite l’absence de candidat: They then bring up the absence of any openly and visibly trans candidate, which keeps them from seeing themselves in the world of federal politics.
Estimant que vivre à Montréal est un pri: Considering living in Montréal a privilege, FrankieB often thinks about the rise of fascism and the far right in the United States and about Americans’ rights regressing a little more each day: “Now, in Canada, we can legally change our gender markers and our names. But what’s the point of being more visible if we don’t have the protection that goes with it?”
Pour FrankieB, le changement doit se con: For FrankieB, change has to be built differently: “I believe we don’t necessarily need a political party to represent us. There are so many organizations doing extraordinary work on the ground, within the population. More means and resources should be given to those who best know the needs of queer people.”
<strong>FLO : « Je sens une montée du fa: FLO: “I feel fascism rising and it scares me”
Flo est non binaire. Barista au Café Vel: Flo is non-binary. A barista at Café Velours, Flo joins us on the outdoor terrace. When asked for their opinion on this election period, a slight sigh first escapes their lips: “I think we’re all scared, especially with everything going on to the south. I feel a slight disengagement in myself from everything that’s happening. I feel fascism rising and it scares me.”
Pour le barista, les partis en lice ne f: For the barista, the parties in the running are not making the effort to listen to the voices of the LGBTQ+ community; the trade war context is taking up all the space. Receptive to the intentions of the MP in their riding, Alexandre Boulerice of the New Democratic Party, Flo will go vote. The NDP is the party closest to their convictions, given its position on the Palestinian genocide.
Pour Flo aussi, le changement doit se fa: For Flo too, change has to happen at the municipal level. That is where concrete action happens, where you can feel comfortable getting involved. “I have few expectations about the changes that might come at the federal level.”
<strong>JUNO : « Comme on tombe dans un: JUNO: “As we slide into a context of economic austerity, it’s often marginalized communities that end up even more marginalized”
Nous croisons Juno sur la rue Sainte-Cat: We run into Juno on Sainte-Catherine Street, in the Village. With his moustache and big smile, he comments with interest on the current political situation. He feels good during this election period. He likes the division that is emerging among the various parties in the running. To him, it may be a sign that the governing party will have a minority.
« Pour moi, ce serait l’occasion d’avoir: “For me, it would be a chance to have more ‘democracy.’ I think it’s a good thing that several viewpoints are being heard right now, and each as loudly as the others,” he explains.
Il réfléchit encore au parti pour lequel: He is still thinking about which party he will vote for. His first choice is the Green Party, but he is still hesitating and wondering whether he will give his vote to the NDP or the Bloc québécois. He nonetheless expresses a few reservations.
« Peu importe qui sera élu, je pense que: “No matter who gets elected, I think minorities will be a little more at risk than they have been in the past. As we slide into a context of economic austerity, it’s often marginalized communities that end up even more marginalized. I’m afraid it’s a cycle that will repeat itself,” he confides.
Lui aussi se dit plus préoccupé par les: He, too, says he is more concerned about the issues that affect his daily life: “Right now, what affects me most is access to housing, the labour shortage, the skyrocketing price of groceries. Everything that mainly affects the middle class.”
<strong>MARIAM : « Je ne suis pas seulem: MARIAM: “I’m not just queer, I’m racialized. I live a reality where I can easily be targeted”
Mariam est l’autre co-propriétaire du Ca: Mariam is the other co-owner of Café Velours. A Canadian of Tunisian origin, she has lived in Canada for about twenty years.
« Quand je suis arrivée ici, j’avais une: “When I arrived here, I had an idea of what Canada’s values were as a country. Twenty years later, I realize it’s only ‘looking good’; the substance of those values is not a daily reality,” she says with a grimace of disgust.
Comme nombre de personnes à qui nous avo: Like many of the people we spoke with, she feels a total disinterest and disengagement from the current political context. Mariam doesn’t yet know who she will vote for. She plans to check the polls at the last minute and make her decision then. “I’m torn. There’s no clear representation. I feel like all the platforms I looked at are outdated, that they’re put in place to look good, and the substance doesn’t speak to me,” she says, pointing to the possibility of a strategic vote.
Les enjeux qui concernent la co-gestionn: The issues that concern the café’s co-manager are many: “I’m not just queer, I’m a racialized queer person. I live a reality where I can easily be targeted. But I have no answers to my questions.”
Elle lève les yeux au ciel : « Je ne me: She rolls her eyes: “I’ve never felt so unsafe. I feel like the political system contributes to that. There’s no strengthening of community ties, of ties between citizens so that we support each other and feel safe. I feel more of a separation, a fragmentation.”
À quelques jours des élections, les élec: A few days before the election, the voters we spoke with are aware of the importance of going to the polls. However, they will go without much conviction. The disconnect between their reality and the world of federal politics, along with the lack of representation, are the main reasons. They all maintain that change must come from an environment closer to their own, the community sphere, where they are already involved.
<em>*FrankieB fait référence au tokenism: *FrankieB is referring to tokenism, a practice of including members of marginalized communities in speeches, workplaces or organizations in a symbolic way, rather than a sincere or real one.
